## Introduction to functions

::: {.incremental}
- Say we want to do something many times
- We could just copy and paste our code, but that gets really dull really quickly
- it also means if we update something, we have to update it in all the duplicate instances of that code
- this gets super dull super quickly
:::

## Solving that problem 

So what we can do is set up a function do repeat a number of steps

Starting simply:

```{r}
x <- 5
y <- 10
z <- 15
```

We want to triple each of our variables and then

We could do x*3, y*3, z*3

## Long hand

```{r}
x_mult <- x * 3
```

But we would have to repeat the code if we wanted to check `y` & `z` and also change all the variables

## Building a function

::: {.incremental}
- we start with naming our function
- we then do all the calculations
- we then return the result
:::

:::{.callout-warning collapse=false appearance='default' icon=true}
A function can only return one result, but later we will be clever in how this 'one result' is built
:::

## The code

```{r}
times_three <- function(input) {
  return(input * 3)
}
```

We can now test it with our variables

```{r}
times_three(x)
times_three(y)
```

## Using any number

We aren't restricted to the pre-determined vectors and can just use a number:

```{r}
times_three(7)
```

## Multiple arguments/parameters

::: {.incremental}
- Although a function can only return one object
- You can add more than one variable into a function separated by commas
:::


```{r}
x_times_y <- function(x, y) {
  result <- x * y
  b <- 150
  return(print(paste0('The answer is ', result, ' and b is ', b)))
}

var <- x_times_y(x, y)

```

## What a function returns

::: {.incremental}
- A function will only return one thing.
- You do not have to specify what it returns with a return function
- R will by default return the last thing in a function
:::

```{r}
x_times_y_no_return <- function(x, y) {
  result <- x * y
  print(paste0('The answer is ', result))
}

x_times_y_no_return(5, 4)

```

## A function's sphere of influence

::: {.incremental}
- What happens in a function's "scope" between `{}` is not in the global environment
- For instance the variable 'result' only exists within the scope of the function
- A function's scope can not affect outside of the function
:::

```{r}
test <- 'monkey'

x_times_y_scope <- function(x, y) {
  result <- x * y
  test <- 'moo'
  print(paste0('The answer is ', test))
}

```

# Guess what will happen?

Before we run this what will happen to the variable 'test'?

```{r}
x_times_y_scope(5, 4)
```

## Multiple steps in a function

```{r}
x_times_y_plus_ten_date <- function(x, y) {
  result <- x * y
  day_of_month <- lubridate::day(Sys.Date())
  dplyr::if_else(day_of_month > 15, result + 10, result)
}

```

Without running it please type into the chat the result of the function

```{r}
x_times_y_plus_ten_date(3, 10)
```

## Functions can be long and/or complicated

::: {.incremental}
- Functions get pretty convoluted pretty quickly and can be hard to read
- which is why it is good practice to write doc strings for functions
- Uses Roxygen and the shortcut Ctrl + Shift + Alt + R for the template
:::

## Function documentation

```{r}

  # This function multiplies two numbers (x and y) and adds 10 to the result
  # if the current day of the month is greater than 15. Otherwise, it simply
  # returns the product of x and y.
  #
  # @param x [numeric] The first number to be multiplied.
  # @param y [numeric] The second number to be multiplied.
  #
  # @return The product of x and y, with 10 added if the current day is past
  # the 15th.
  #
  # @examples
  # Example 1: Today is the 10th of the month
  # x <- 5
  # y <- 2
  # result <- x_times_y_plus_ten_date(x, y)
  # print(result) # Output: 10
  #
  # Example 2: Today is the 20th of the month
  # x <- 3
  # y <- 4
  # result <- x_times_y_plus_ten_date(x, y)
  # print(result) # Output: 22
x_times_y_plus_ten_date <- function(x, y) {
  result <- x * y
  day_of_month <- lubridate::day(Sys.Date())
  dplyr::if_else(day_of_month > 15, result + 10, result)
}

```

## Over to you

- Tweak the previous function so that instead of "times the first two inputs and add 10 to the result based on the day in the month" it adds a number you specify (another variable)
- For bonus points assign your result to a variable


```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
countdown::countdown(
  minutes = 7,
  color_border = "#005EB8",
  color_text = "#005EB8",
  color_running_text = "white",
  color_running_background = "#005EB8",
  color_finished_text = "#005EB8",
  color_finished_background = "white",
  margin = "0.9em",
  font_size = "2em"
)
```

## Answer - Altering a function

```{r}
x_times_y_plus_ten_date <- function(x, y, add) {
  result <- x * y
  day_of_month <- lubridate::day(Sys.Date())
  dplyr::if_else(day_of_month > 15, result + add, result)
}

variable <- x_times_y_plus_ten_date(4, 1, 15)
variable
```


## Applying data to functions

We can apply our made up new functions to a dataframe we first create:

```{r}
library(NHSRdatasets)

data <- NHSRdatasets::ae_attendances

data_fun <- data |>
  dplyr::filter(org_code %in% c('RQM', 'RJ1', 'RDD'), type == '1') |>
  dplyr::select(-breaches)

```

## Using a function to add data to a column

```{r}
#| code-line-numbers: "4"
data_fun |>
  dplyr::rowwise() |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    attend_times_admit_maybe_plus_ten = x_times_y_plus_ten_date(
      attendances,
      admissions,
      10
    )
  )

```

This is a bit of a silly example but shows what potentially can be done.

This can be great for calculating rates, for example, per 10,000

## Creating a function to plot SPC

We can write a lot of code that will be reused for multiple sites into one function:

```{r}
plot_site <- function(site) {
  # we now want to create a for each attendance type
  data_spc <- data |>
    dplyr::filter(org_code == site) # note this is where we are using our 'site'
  # variable

  # turn our ptd_spc into an object
  plot_spc <- data_spc |>
    NHSRplotthedots::ptd_spc(
      value_field = attendances,
      date_field = period,
      improvement_direction = 'decrease',
      facet_field = type
    )
  
  # feed that object into ptd_create_ggplot

  return(
    plot_spc |>
      NHSRplotthedots::ptd_create_ggplot(
        fixed_y_axis_multiple = FALSE,
        x_axis_date_format = "%b %y",
        x_axis_breaks = "2 months"
      )
  )
}

```

## Apply the plot function to code

```{r}
plot_site(site ='RJ1')

plot_site(site = 'RDD')

```

:::{.callout-wardning collapse=false appearance='default' icon=true}
- This function is bad practice as it relies on `data` existing already
- If this data changed name or needed to be something else the function would break
:::

## Adding another argument for data

This has a new argument but also pre-set for `RJ1` and a df called `data`

```{r}
#| code-line-numbers: "2"
plot_site <- function(site = 'RJ1', 
                      df = data) {
  # this is where we set a default

  # we now want to create a for each attendance type
  data_spc <- df |> # note this is where pulling in our data
    dplyr::filter(org_code == site)

  # turn our ptd_spc into an object
  plot_spc <- data_spc |>
    NHSRplotthedots::ptd_spc(
      value_field = attendances,
      date_field = period,
      improvement_direction = 'decrease',
      facet_field = type
    )

  # feed that object into ptd_create_ggplot

  return(
    plot_spc |>
      NHSRplotthedots::ptd_create_ggplot(
        fixed_y_axis_multiple = FALSE,
        x_axis_date_format = "%b %y",
        x_axis_breaks = "2 months"
      )
  )
}

```

## No changes to the use

This works just the same as the data is still referred to, but in the argument

```{r}
plot_site()
```

But, if needed we could change the data source and site to something else:

```{r}
new_data <- data

plot_site(df = new_data,
          site = "RDU")
```
